entries.title: Databricks vs. Oracle in 2026
entries.summary: Why organizations are moving beyond OracleEnterprise data warehouses built on Oracle...
entries.content:
The modern lakehouse vs. the legacy data warehouse

Enterprise data warehouses built on Oracle served organizations well for decades. But the demands of modern data and AI have outgrown the capabilities of traditional warehouse architectures. Organizations today need a platform that unifies analytics, data engineering, AI, and real-time workloads without the cost complexity, vendor lock-in, and architectural fragmentation that come with legacy systems.

Databricks provides a fundamentally different approach: an open, unified lakehouse architecture that consolidates BI, ETL, streaming, machine learning, and generative AI on a single governed platform. No more separate data warehouses, data lakes, ML platforms, and streaming systems. You get it all in one place, so you can easily power every workload or latency.

  • Complete open foundation. Databricks is built on open formats (Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg™), so your data is never trapped in a proprietary system. Oracle stores data in proprietary formats that create deep dependencies on Oracle tooling, licensing, and infrastructure.
  • One platform for every workload. Databricks runs BI, ETL, streaming, ML, and AI on the same governed data. Oracle requires separate systems, add-on licenses, and constant data movement between analytics, operational, and AI environments.
  • Lower cost, predictable at scale. Databricks separates storage and compute on cloud object storage, with serverless scaling and zero cost when idle. Oracle's ECPU-based pricing, autoscaling up to 3× base capacity, and complex licensing make costs difficult to predict as you grow.
  • Embedded AI in the platform. Databricks is a better-suited platform for building and deploying AI, with native capabilities such as model serving, agent development, and natural-language analytics directly into the lakehouse. Oracle's AI capabilities are newer, less mature, and require additional configuration and licensing.

Genie, Agent Bricks, Native AI functions, MLflow, model serving, AI Search; all on governed lakehouse data

Oracle ML (limited), AI Vector Search (newer), requires separate configuration and licensing

Native Structured Streaming, CDC, Lakehouse// RT for sub-second analytics

GoldenGate (separate license), limited native streaming capabilities

Data sharing

OpenSharing: open protocol for cross-platform, cross-cloud data sharing

No native open sharing protocol for on-premises; limited OpenSharing support in cloud deployments

Multi-cloud

AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud

Primarily OCI; limited multicloud support with Cloud@Customer

Migration tooling

Lakebridge with automated code conversion via Genie Code

N/A. Oracle is typically the source, not the destination, of modern migrations

BI & analytics

AI/BI with Genie (natural-language analytics), no per-seat licensing

Oracle Analytics (separate product and license)

Databricks is open by design and stores 100% of customer data in open formats (Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg™) on the customer's own cloud object storage. This means:

  • No proprietary lock-in. Your data can be read by any engine that supports open formats, including Spark, Trino, Presto, dbt, and any Iceberg-compatible tool.
  • You own your storage. Data lives in your S3, ADLS, or GCS account. You control access, retention, and portability.
  • Cross-engine governance. Unity Catalog provides a single catalog that works across engines, clouds, and tools with consistent permissions, lineage, and auditing.
  • Open sharing. OpenSharing enables governed data sharing across organizations and platforms without copying data.

Oracle stores data in a proprietary binary format with limited support for open formats, and its reliance on PL/SQL, Oracle-specific tooling, and Exadata infrastructure for peak performance creates deep vendor dependencies that make migration, portability, and multicloud strategies costly and complex.

Databricks is designed for cost efficiency at scale:

  • Separation of storage and compute. Store unlimited data in inexpensive cloud object storage. Scale compute independently and pay nothing when warehouses are idle.
  • SQL Serverless warehouses. Instant startup, automatic scaling, and per-second billing eliminate overprovisioning.
  • Photon engine. Vectorized execution delivers industry-leading query performance for faster results on less compute.
  • Predictive Optimization. The platform automatically tunes file sizes, clustering, and statistics. No need for DBA tuning marathons or specialist consultants.
  • No add-on licensing. Governance (Unity Catalog), BI (AI/BI), orchestration (Lakeflow Jobs), and the SQL editor are included.
  • No per-seat BI licensing. AI/BI with Genie provides natural-language analytics without per-user fees.

Oracle's pricing is more complex. ECPU-based compute that can autoscale to 3× your base capacity, add-on licensing for essential features like GoldenGate and Database Vault, and annual support fees that compound year over year make the total cost of ownership difficult to predict and control as you scale.

Organizations that have migrated from Oracle to Databricks have reported significant cost reductions. AXA Japan, for example, achieved a 60% reduction in warehouse costs and 70% lower ETL costs after migrating from legacy Oracle and Redshift environments to Databricks. 

We wanted one integrated tool to manage our data from infrastructure to BI to AI use cases, and at the same time reduce running costs. - Nicolas Hebrant, CDO, AXA Japan

Databricks was built for data and AI. The lakehouse architecture means AI workloads run directly on the same governed data that powers BI and analytics. This means no copies or separate infrastructure:

  • Enrich data with AI directly in SQL. Run sentiment analysis, classification, summarization, and extraction on lakehouse data.
  • Track experiments and manage models in one place. MLflow handles experiment tracking, model registry, and deployment end-to-end — built in.
  • Deploy models to production in minutes. Serve models at scale with built-in endpoints that support all major foundation models. 
  • Build and deploy production AI agents at scale. Create agents that take autonomous actions grounded in your enterprise data, with built-in controls for quality, cost, and compliance.
  • Give every business user direct access to data insights. Genie lets anyone ask questions in natural language and get trusted, governed answers.
  • Power RAG, recommendations, and semantic search natively. Vector indexing and similarity search run directly on your lakehouse data. No external vector database needed.
  • Ground external AI agents in your enterprise data. Managed MCP servers let third-party agents query your lakehouse securely, without exposing raw data or building custom integrations.
  • Govern AI with the same rigor as your data. Unity Catalog extends lineage, access control, and auditability across ML models, AI agents, features, and endpoints. Unity AI Gateway adds centralized rate limiting, cost controls, and usage tracking across all foundation model APIs, so you can manage AI spend and enforce policies from a single pane of glass.

Oracle has added AI Vector Search and in-database ML to its Autonomous Database, but these capabilities are newer (the Autonomous AI Lakehouse launched in October 2025), require additional configuration and licensing, and lack equivalents to Databricks' MLflow, Agent Bricks, or Genie with no unified governance across data, models, and agents.

Oracle

Unified catalog

Database-level catalog — no unified governance across AI, agents, or external tools

Limited lineage within Oracle ecosystem

Primarily OCI-centric

No comparison is complete without acknowledging where Oracle remains strong. Oracle has decades of investment in high-concurrency OLTP, mission-critical transactional systems, and deep integration with its own application ecosystem. For certain workloads, that maturity matters.

  • High-concurrency OLTP. Oracle Database and Exadata are battle-tested for thousands of concurrent transactional reads and writes with strict latency guarantees — the kind of workload that powers core banking, order management, and ERP systems.
  • Mission-critical transactional applications. Features like Real Application Clusters (RAC), Data Guard, and Exadata's storage offload provide high availability, disaster recovery, and performance characteristics that enterprises have relied on for decades.
  • Oracle-dependent enterprise systems. Organizations running Oracle E-Business Suite, PeopleSoft, Siebel, or Oracle Fusion have deep dependencies on Oracle Database as the system of record. Replacing the database layer in these environments is rarely practical or advisable.

Databricks recognizes that analytics and AI don't exist in isolation from operational data. Lakebase, a serverless Postgres-compatible database built into the Databricks Platform, is Databricks' answer to the operational data gap. Lakebase unifies OLTP and OLAP on a single governed layer, eliminating the need to move data between operational and analytical systems. 

Lakebase is purpose-built for three workloads at the intersection of operational and analytical data:

  • Serving lakehouse-curated data to applications at millisecond latency (reverse ETL without the ETL)
  • Powering online feature stores for real-time ML inference
  • Storing application and AI agent state — conversation memory, workflow sign-off, pipeline metadata.

It's ideal for existing Databricks customers who want to eliminate the separate operational database, ETL pipeline, and governance model that traditionally sit between their lakehouse and their applications.

Lakebase is not a replacement for Oracle's core OLTP engine. If your Oracle environment powers mission-critical, high-volume transactional systems (i.e. core banking, ERP, order management) with strict latency guarantees at scale, Oracle (or a dedicated OLTP database) remains the right choice for those specific workloads. Lakebase is designed for the growing category of data-intensive and AI-driven applications that need fast, governed access to lakehouse data without the complexity of a separate database stack.

The practical takeaway: If your Oracle environment is primarily an analytical data warehouse or reporting platform, Databricks is the clear modernization path. If Oracle is your OLTP backbone for mission-critical applications, it may remain the right choice for those specific workloads while Databricks becomes the platform for everything analytical, AI-driven, and forward-looking. And as Lakebase matures, even that line will continue to shift.

Databricks offers a migration agent, powered by Genie Code, that uses AI to automate and accelerate data platform migrations from Oracle to Databricks, reducing complexity and manual effort. It covers the full migration lifecycle, from assessment to data validation. With this migration tool, you get:

  • Agentic conversion loop. Rather than a one-shot transpile, the AI agent runs a plan → convert → validate → fix cycle - analyzing source files, generating conversions, detecting errors, and iteratively repairing failed sections until the output is correct.
  • Concurrent multi-file conversion. Launch parallel subagents to convert entire folders of Oracle SQL simultaneously, with project-level tracking of conversion status across hundreds of files.
  • Side-by-side review. Every conversion produces a source-to-target diff, so engineers can review exactly what changed and approve or adjust before committing.
  • Lineage-aware migration planning. Visualize code complexity and dependency graphs to identify interdependent objects that must be migrated together.
  • Custom conversion rules. Encode business rules, proprietary data types, naming standards, and preferred Databricks patterns as custom Genie Code skills so the agent learns your organization's conventions.
  • Flexible output. Generates either ANSI-compatible Databricks Lakehouse or Databricks Notebooks using the DataFrame API, matching your team's preferred development style.

This agent supports a wide range of sources, including Oracle, T-SQL, Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery, and Teradata. It is available directly in the Databricks workspace.

Customers who have migrated from Oracle Exadata to Databricks have witnessed 40% faster time to insights, up to 4x SQL performance improvements, and significant cost savings.

Yes. Databricks Lakehouse provides full data warehousing capabilities — including ANSI SQL, materialized views, stored procedures, fine-grained security, and BI tool connectivity, while also supporting ETL, streaming, ML, and AI on the same platform.

Yes. Databricks Lakehouse connects natively to Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Qlik, and other major BI tools via JDBC/ODBC. Databricks also offers AI/BI with Genie for natural-language analytics with no per-seat licensing.

Migration timelines vary based on complexity, but Databricks provides automated assessment and code conversion tools with Databricks Migration Agent that significantly accelerate the process. Many organizations complete initial migrations in weeks, with full production cutover in months.

Databricks Lakehouse scripting provides stored procedure functionality that covers the vast majority of PL/SQL use cases. For complex Oracle-specific logic, BladeBridge automates code conversion and identifies areas requiring manual attention.

Oracle annual support and licensing fees compound over time. Migrating to Databricks eliminates Oracle licensing entirely and replaces it with consumption-based DBU pricing. This means that when you use Databricks, you pay only for what you use.

Yes. Databricks provides native Structured Streaming, CDC via Lakeflow Connect, and Lakehouse Real-Time for sub-second, high-concurrency analytical queries. Those same capabilities require separate GoldenGate licensing in Oracle.

Absolutely. Databricks supports Lakehouse Federation, which lets you query Oracle data directly from Databricks without moving it. This enables a phased migration where you can run both systems in parallel.

Yes. Databricks supports open model choice (Claude, Llama, GPT-OSS, Gemini, and fine-tunes) behind a single gateway, rather than a single-vendor model bet.

entries.summary: For the past two years, the story around enterprise AI adoption has mostly been about...
entries.content:
How to measure and manage AI costs.

  • Enterprises are shifting from "tokenmaxxing" to "valuemaxxing," measuring the impact generated per dollar spent on AI.
  • Measuring AI ROI requires attribution granular enough to trace spend to a user, team, project or even a single pull request
  • Spend guardrails, end-to-end observability and a centralized point all AI traffic flows through are the foundation teams need now

For the past two years, the story around enterprise AI adoption has mostly been about getting people to use it. Over the past few months, that story has rapidly been changing in many organizations. AI observability that once measured success by token volume is starting to measure success by return on investment, and the enterprises that figure out cost management first are the ones that will be able to scale AI without their spend outrunning their revenue.

At its core, AI cost management is the practice of measuring, attributing, controlling and optimizing AI spend across models, agents, applications and teams. The goal isn't simply to use fewer tokens, but to maximize the business value generated for every dollar spent. As AI agents take on more autonomous work, that discipline increasingly extends to managing the cost of agent reasoning, tool calls, and the models powering them.

We sat down with Kevin Stumpf, a Senior Staff Engineer at Databricks and Technical Lead for Unity Gateway, to talk through how teams should actually put that discipline into practice: not treating AI cost as a line item to minimize, but as a system to manage.

Social media is full of leaders arguing that "tokenmaxxing," running AI as hard and as often as possible, is the right way to accelerate innovation. Other than the obvious cost implications, why is that the wrong way to think about AI adoption?

Kevin Stumpf: The industry is moving from tokenmaxxing to valuemaxxing. In the early days, there were public leaderboards showing how many tokens people were burning through, and that made sense as a strategy at the time. A lot of people were reluctant to start using AI, so showing that the leaders everyone looked up to were heavy AI users gave others a reason to follow. If I see someone I respect using a ton of AI, I want to be like that person.

But the system got gamed. Once being at the top of the leaderboard became a status symbol, people figured out the fastest way to get there wasn't good work, it was volume. Spin up a dumb agent that runs in a loop, have it ask what the weather is over and over, and burn through tokens doing essentially nothing. That was the predictable outcome of an incentive structure that rewarded raw usage instead of outcomes.

Now that organizations are broadly bought into AI, the conversation has shifted to responsible, effective use. What we should really be building toward is a different kind of leaderboard, one that ranks people by the impact they generated with AI divided by what it cost to generate it. That's return on investment, and it's a much harder thing to quantify than raw token counts, but it's the number that actually matters. Related: What’s Driving Enterprise AI Adoption?

Can you walk us through what "cost attribution" really means in AI?

Kevin Stumpf: AI cost attribution is ultimately about answering two questions: where does my spend come from, and what did I get for it? At the simplest level, that means attributing cost to an individual user or a team, like a data science team or a software engineering team. It can also map to a specific project, or to a node in an org chart, like understanding how much spend sits under a VP of AI versus an SVP of engineering.

The goal is granular enough visibility that you can slice and dice the data and understand where cost is actually coming from, because you can't manage what you can't measure. Databricks provides cost attribution out of the box by user, group, agent, AI gateway endpoint, model, provider and time period. But organizations can also hyper-customize it using request-level tags. A tag can represent anything your organization cares about, like a specific pull request, a feature or an external customer, and once every request carries that tag, you can aggregate spend against it however you need to.

That shift in customer sentiment has been real. Six months ago, the top concern was falling behind on AI adoption. Now it's the opposite: AI is often used for silly things, costs are growing faster than revenue, and leaders are asking how to bend that cost curve before it eats into profitability. This isn't a hypothetical. It's a boardroom-level conversation at nearly every organization we talk to, including internally at Databricks.

Token usage and context window size get blamed a lot, but are rarely explained well. What does context bloat actually look like in a production system, and what's the practical fix?

Kevin Stumpf: Context bloat means throwing far more information at an agent than it needs to make a good decision. That's a problem for two reasons. First, it burns unnecessary tokens. Second, it's distracting: the agent has to process that extra information and decide whether it's relevant, which is its own kind of overhead. It's not unlike handing a person a stack of irrelevant documents and asking them to figure out what matters before they can even start the task.

The best fix isn't trimming or caching after the fact, it's not generating the bloat in the first place. A common and effective pattern is letting the agent pull relevant context on demand, through tools, MCP servers or skills, rather than proactively pushing everything it might need up front. You should only push context to an agent by default if you're 90% certain or more that it's genuinely important for the task at hand. Otherwise, let the agent know what's available and allow it to fetch what it needs when it needs it.

Model selection is often a "pick once" decision. Why should it be dynamic instead, and how does intelligent routing decide, in real time, whether a task needs a frontier model or something cheaper and faster? Does that same idea extend to choosing between different agent harnesses?

Kevin Stumpf: AI cost optimization isn't about always choosing the cheapest model, and teams should shift to choosing the lowest-cost model or harness that can deliver the quality a task requires. The reality right now is that frontier models are highly capable and expensive, while non-frontier models are still very capable, just less expensive. Roughly 5 to 10% of tasks genuinely need a frontier model, either because the stakes are high enough that you want the best possible outcome, or because the problem is too complex for anything less. The other 90% of tasks are solvable by lesser models, whether that's open source models you host yourself or cheaper model families from the major labs.

Left to their own incentives, most employees will default to the most expensive model available, because their goal is simply to get the problem solved, and nobody is watching what it costs them individually. Smart Routing solves that by inserting a layer that assesses task complexity in real time and decides whether a request should go to a frontier model or a lower-cost one, with the goal of maintaining the same quality output at a lower cost.

Harness routing is the next layer beyond model routing. There's emerging research showing that the exact same model, run through a different harness, can produce meaningfully different costs. That makes sense, because the harness determines how the model interacts with its environment: what rules it follows, when it compacts the context window, what business logic governs its behavior. All of that directly affects how many tokens get spent. Harness routing is the next step in that crawl-walk-run evolution of cost optimization, which we enable through Unity Gateway and Omnigent, our meta-harness.

Let's talk about guardrails on spend itself, like hard caps, budgets, and rate limits. What's the right way to design these so they stop runaway costs without hurting developer productivity or breaking production workflows?

Kevin Stumpf: Some rules apply to every organization, and others depend on the use case or the company. Everyone should have hard spend caps in place to catch runaway usage. If your typical power user spends around $300 a day on AI at most, set the hard cap somewhat above that, maybe $500. That gap gives you room to catch genuine errors, like an agent that got left running in a loop by accident, without capping off legitimate high-usage days.

Beyond that baseline, differentiated budgets by team or project make a lot of sense. A team working on something critical for the CEO might warrant a much higher budget than a team working on lower-priority work, and that decision should weigh the value of what that team produces against the cost of giving them more headroom.

Budgets should also be able to trigger different types of responses, not just a hard stop. They can send alerts, apply hard caps or reduce available model capacity, for example cutting off default access to frontier models once a team has burned through 70% of its budget and routing the rest of their requests to open source models instead. The core principles that apply everywhere: prevent runaway spend, set differentiated limits by group or project, alert before you cap and build in intelligent capacity reduction rather than an abrupt shutoff.

REPORT

The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise

Which platforms offer agent monitoring and cost tracking together, and how far can that visibility take you toward measuring actual ROI, not just spend?

Kevin Stumpf: Measuring cost is a lot easier than connecting that cost to return on investment, and that's the question everyone wants answered and almost nobody has fully solved yet. Session or request-level tagging is what makes this possible. If an agent is working on a specific pull request, it can tag its session or specific requests it generates with that pull request's identifier. That attribution flows back into a cost dashboard, so you can see, for example, that a given pull request cost $300 to complete. This is something we’re already doing internally at Databricks.

In an ideal state, and this is something we're building into the Unity Gateway product. You can go a step further and connect that pull request to a specific feature, and that feature to a measurable outcome, like how much revenue or pipeline it generated in a given period. That's the holy grail: not just knowing what AI cost, but knowing what it returned. With Unity Gateway, we already have a highly customizable platform to build this on, and we're investing in making that cost-to-return view available out of the box rather than something teams have to construct themselves.

For a company running multiple models, agents and tools across many teams, what does good spend visibility actually require? Is it a dashboard problem, a governance problem or a FinOps problem?

Kevin Stumpf: Good spend visibility requires that every AI interaction flows through a centralized system. That's what allows you to lock down the right information consistently, so you can build reliable dashboards and alerts on top of it. An AI gateway provides a centralized control point for AI cost management across models, agents, tools and teams. Databricks Unity Gateway is designed to provide that centralized control point across models, agents, tools and coding agents. When AI interactions flow through a common control point, organizations can observe usage, attribute costs, enforce budgets and optimize spend in one place.

But having the centralized system isn't enough on its own. You also need a way to enforce that everyone actually routes their AI traffic through it. Visibility only works if adoption is universal, not optional.

Cost control can't come at the expense of quality or reliability. How do you know when an optimization has gone too far and started hurting output?

Kevin Stumpf: That's genuinely use case specific. You need a feedback mechanism, and it can be either subjective or objective. Subjective feedback is anecdotal, someone on the team telling you they can't get the job done within the current budget. That's fast to get but easy to dismiss as one person's complaint. Objective feedback comes from automated evaluations, which are harder to set up but far more reliable.

For a common use case like coding agents, that might mean defining a proxy metric for quality, such as merged pull requests that don't get rolled back within two weeks. From there, you can experiment: cut the budget in half and see whether that gold star metric moves, holds steady or even improves, since constraints sometimes breed creativity. Running parallel experiments across teams with different budgets, models and harnesses, or time-bound comparisons over a few weeks, lets you infer whether a given budget is creating value or destroying it, rather than guessing.

What role does end-to-end tracing and monitoring play here? Once you can see prompts, tool calls and token usage across an entire agent workflow, what does that unlock that you couldn't do before?

Kevin Stumpf: Tracing is about collecting the full exhaust of what agents are doing: what they're thinking, what tools they're calling, what data they're pulling in, whether the prompts are good or bad. That raw data is what you can mine for insight, whether that's identifying abuse, waste, security leaks or simply patterns you never thought to look for.

This mirrors what happened in the broader data industry. Early on, we only had clean, structured data in databases. Then came data lakes, which for a while became data swamps because people dumped unstructured data into them without a way to extract value from it. Eventually those swamps turned back into usable data lakes, and now we're in a better position than ever to extract insight from unstructured and semi-structured data, largely because LLMs are flexible enough to process it. Agent traces fall into that same category. The more of it you collect, the more insight becomes available, and it's easier to get to than it's ever been.

A lot of enterprises are moving from single AI applications to fleets of agents. Does that shift change the cost equation (new cost drivers? new blind spots?) compared to running one model behind one app?

Kevin Stumpf: It doesn't change the equation so much as it multiplies it. Agent swarms are going to be the new reality, and every one of those agents will be spending tokens that need to be attributed, monitored and managed. Right now is the time to put the right cost visibility and management foundation in place, before the number of agents in production grows the way it's projected to.

Coding agents are the dominant category burning tokens today, but that's going to expand into many other classes of agents doing autonomous work around the clock, agents calling other agents calling other agents. Organizations that wait to build centralized AI observability and cost management infrastructure until that complexity arrives will be building it under pressure, instead of on their own terms.

If you had to leave enterprise AI leaders with one mindset shift about cost management heading into next year, what would it be?

Kevin Stumpf: I wouldn't wait for next year. This is urgent, and it should be treated that way starting now. If I had to boil it down to a single idea, it's this: you can't manage what you don't measure. That applies to raw materials, it applies to people, and it applies to AI just as much. AI is quickly becoming one of the most important line items on a company's cash flow statement, and it needs to be fully instrumented so it can be measured and, in turn, managed. It's just another raw ingredient in the system that produces your organization's goods or services, and it deserves to be treated with the same discipline.

The clock starts now Controlling AI costs across teams using multiple models and tools isn't a problem that gets solved with a single dashboard or a one-time model choice. It's an operating discipline: attribution granular enough to trace spend to a person or a project, routing that adapts in real time to what a task requires, guardrails that catch runaway spend before it becomes a headline and tracing detailed enough to turn raw usage data into real insight. The organizations getting ahead of this aren't the ones spending the least on AI. They're the ones who can say, with confidence, exactly what they got for what they spent.

entries.content:
Augmenting your first line of defense with knowledge, tools and context.

by Razi Bayati and Anthony Melnick

  • As fraudsters use agentic AI to attack at machine speed, defense teams must accelerate response times using AI coworkers. Additionally, real-time network telemetry can be used as fraud signals and improve fraud detection models.
  • Databricks unifies Fraud detection stack on a single platform: Lakebase removes the analytical and transactional split for faster data sync, Databricks Apps powers a custom case-management workbench, and Genie as an AI coworker, provides natural-language querying over governed fraud data; This unified stack supports fraud detection team to work more efficiently against fraudsters.
  • Our Telecom Fraud Prevention Solution Accelerator deploys this entire pipeline, risk engine, workbench, and AI investigation agent into your workspace via Databricks Asset Bundles, adaptable to other industries.

Background

According to the Communications Fraud Control Association's 2025 survey, telecom fraud losses have climbed to $41.82 billion1, and the broader fraud economy is growing fast: U.S. consumers alone reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, a 25% jump in a single year2. Breaches are getting more expensive too; the global average cost of a data breach hit a record $4.88 million in 20243; Every dollar of fraud costs a carrier roughly 3.4x once you count chargebacks, replacement costs, and the operational overhead of investigating it.

A telecom account is no longer just a phone plan. It's the gateway to many assets that a subscriber owns: banking apps authenticate through phone number, password resets flow through it, and two-factor codes land on it. Consequently, when a fraudster compromises an account through phishing, social engineering, or using credentials from an old breach, the clock runs fast. Within minutes they can execute a SIM swap, change the billing address, order expensive devices, and pivot into linked financial accounts often before the victim or the carrier notices anything at all. Meanwhile, the fraud team is still waiting on last night's batch job to complete.

That dichotomy, fraud moving at machine speed while detection moves at batch speed, is the inhibitor. For an executive team, fraud is not a security footnote. It’s revenue leakage, regulatory exposure, accelerated churn, and an operations tax that rarely shows up cleanly in a loss report. Every major fraud type succeeds for one of three reasons:

  • It creates a data signature that has not been detected in time
  • It exploits gaps between systems that don't talk to each other
  • Or it thrives in the lag of batch processing.

Here's the reframe we think matters most: All three are data architecture problems that can be solved with a unified, real-time, governed data foundation.

Account takeover and SIM swap attacks were up 240% in 2024 in Australia based on stockhead , and roughly 90% of them now happen with no contact with the actual victim. The fraudster's request simply looks legitimate. International Revenue Share Fraud pumps $4–7 billion a year into premium-rate numbers by looking like normal traffic. SIM box bypass fraud (~$3.1B/year) hides inside call patterns that seem routine1.

In nearly every case, the signal that would detect this fraud already exists - it's just split across the six or seven systems (CDRs, CRM, billing, device/SIM, network, digital channel logs) that don't share a single query surface. Often sophisticated fraud types are processed in overnight batches when the attack window is measured in minutes while simpler fraud types such as spoofing can be caught real time.

The human cost of that fragmentation compounds the financial one. Rigid rule-based systems flood analysts with false positives, so fraud teams spend hours investigating benign account changes while the sophisticated attacks executing at machine speed slip through. It's a daunting cycle: analysts drowning in alerts, genuine threats going undetected, losses mounting.

Most operators have invested heavily in fraud management systems that successfully block the known, well-understood attack patterns, and those systems are saving real money today. The opportunity isn't to rip those out, it's to augment them. But fraud is an adversarial game, not a static one — every pattern a model learns to catch is a pattern fraudsters are actively working to route around, and they do it fast. The gaps show up in exactly what existing fraud engines were never built for: cross-channel correlation, behavioral modeling, device emulation, and fraud patterns that evolve faster than a rule-change cycle can keep up with. Those gaps trace back to architecture, not effort — and architecture that can't move at the speed of the adversary is architecture that's already behind.

The common thread in any anti-fraud system is that it will undergo adversarial drift, and it will happen on the fraudster's timeline, not yours. The moment a fraudster gets caught, they change behavior immediately — no delay, no courtesy window. That means the recall of any deployed model starts degrading right away, sometimes within 24 hours. In this environment, being outdated isn't a minor inefficiency, it's the difference between a model that catches fraud and one that's effectively blind to it. There is no such thing as "good enough for now" — a detection system is only as good as its last update, and the agility of the monitor-tune-redeploy loop isn't a nice-to-have, it's the whole game.

This is exactly where most fraud operations lose the race. The typical pattern: an operational (OLTP) system handles live transactions, while a separate analytical (OLAP) system houses the actual intelligence: — the context, the historical queries, the fraud models, the dashboards data scientists refine every day. The problem is that the live risk engine can't reach into that analytical environment fast enough at decision time. Teams must then fall back on a slow, costly synchronization process — scheduled batch jobs that copy finished "gold" data (engineered features, model scores, risk signals) out of the OLAP warehouse and back into the operational database.

That copying is the bottleneck, and in an adversarial-drift world, bottlenecks are where you lose. The operational store is always working off a stale snapshot — and "stale" compounds fast when your adversary is actively mutating behavior hour by hour. The pipeline is brittle (a schema change upstream breaks it), expensive to maintain, and worst of all, slow to repair;every hour it's down is an hour your decision engine is running on yesterday's intelligence against today's attack. The models and context that make detection smart end up stranded one hop away from the decision engine, exactly when speed matters most.

Put an AI agent on top and it inherits the same gap, just with higher stakes: either it reasons without the rich OLAP context it needs — fast but blind — or you copy sensitive gold data out to reach it, trading governance for access. Neither option holds up against an adversary that's already moved on by the time your architecture catches up.

The fix has to attack the actual bottleneck: the hop between where intelligence lives and where decisions get made. Lakebase, our managed Postgres engine integrated into the unified environment, eliminates the traditional OLTP/OLAP split entirely. Gold tables in the lakehouse sync continuously into Lakebase, giving the real-time scoring engine sub-millisecond feature retrieval — right alongside the same analytical models that generated them. There's no batch job standing between the decision engine and the intelligence it needs, which means no stale snapshot and no brittle pipeline waiting to break on the next schema change. When a model starts drifting, the fix propagates at the speed the drift demands, not at the speed of the next scheduled sync.

Meanwhile, our agentic platform and Genie let analysts analyze historical incidents, synthesize operational playbooks, and automate complex investigative work — closing the monitor-tune-redeploy loop faster, so the gap between "fraudster changes behavior" and "model adapts" shrinks from days to something much closer to real time. With Databricks Apps, teams can rapidly deploy custom operational tools on this same unified architecture, instead of waiting on a separate build cycle every time a new fraud pattern demands a new tool.

And because it's one architecture rather than two systems stitched together, an AI agent built on top doesn't face the earlier trade-off between reasoning with rich context and preserving governance. A single plane under Unity Catalog manages governance, lineage, and security from raw network ingestion through to the live transaction decision — so speed and control stop being opposites. Compliance leaders get full lineage, engineering teams get an architecture that can actually keep pace with an adversary that doesn't wait around.

Databricks built a Solution Accelerator for telecom fraud, covering the full lifecycle from raw data to an analyst queue to the executive dashboard.

The pipeline. The solution includes a pipeline with a medallion architecture (Bronze → Silver → Gold) that generates realistic transaction, device, and network Call Detail Record data at scale.

Additionally, a risk engine scores every transaction against rules like impossible travel, cell/IP mismatch, rapid cell-tower hops, roaming anomalies, and device emulation, the same category of signals that catch SIM box and SIM-swap fraud in production. Score threshold route transactions to one of three outcomes: auto-approve, queue for analyst review, or auto-block.

The fraud analyst workbench app showcases different fraud workflows with three role-based views built on the same governed data:

  • Executive - financial P&L impact, quarterly trends, regional risk distribution, and a Genie Space for a leader to ask questions in natural language like "which regions had the most SIM-swap cases this quarter?" and get governed, data-backed answers - no analyst or SQL required.
  • Management - Ticket pipeline health, a 30-day AI forecast, fraud engine performance, and SLA tracking, so managers can staff analyst capacity proactively instead of reactively.
  • Analyst - a case queue and device/case detail view backed by a tool-calling AI investigation Genie agent that reads case history, risk rules, and policy together, then recommends approve, deny, or escalate - and a Knowledge Assistant trained on the company's fraud playbook for procedural questions like escalation thresholds and documentation standards.

None of the individual pieces here - a risk-scoring pipeline, an AI agent, a governed catalog - are unique. What's different is running all of them on one platform instead of stitching together a fraud engine, a separate feature store, a BI tool, and a bolted-on AI layer, each with its own governance model and its own latency tax. For telecom operators, the opportunity is huge. It's recognizing that the infrastructure built to protect the business is the same infrastructure that can turn network data into a new revenue line.

  • Clone it, deploy the pipeline, and stand up the analyst workbench in your own workspace - the industry-specific logic lives in a single configuration file, so the same architecture retargets to fintech, insurance, or e-commerce fraud with no changes to the core platform.
  • To go deeper, reach out to your Databricks account team to provision Lakebase, creating synced tables, configuring a fraud-domain Genie Space, and building the investigation app.

entries.summary: In this conversation, Catherine Brown talks with Patrick about what happened when...
entries.content:
Databricks co-founder Patrick Wendell on why AI coding costs grow exponentially, and how engineering leaders can bend the curve without slowing their teams down

  • The cost curve is structural. AI tools are consumption-priced, so usage grows exponentially while revenue doesn’t. Unlimited tokens and hard spend caps both fail, and Databricks has moved to visibility plus progressive friction instead.
  • Four levers cut unit costs by as much as 90%. Shift defaults to more efficient models, route each task to the cheapest model that can handle it, give developers visibility into their spend, and cut token overhead. Token price alone is a poor predictor of what a model actually costs.
  • Every engineering org needs a control layer. An AI gateway sits between developers and models to handle access, routing, budgets, and tracing, making AI spend observable, steerable, and predictable.

In this conversation, Catherine Brown talks with Patrick about what happened when Databricks went all in on AI coding agents: how costs initially spiraled with growing usage , what actually brought unit costs down by as much as 90%, and why every engineering organization needs a control layer between its developers and its models. That control layer started as an internal fix for Databricks' own AI bill, and it became the inspiration for Unity Gateway.

Catherine: You run Databricks' AI products, and you've also been the internal champion for AI adoption. Why has this become such a personal priority for you?

Patrick: Because engineering output is the main bottleneck in our business. Every company needs its engineering team to move faster, and if you can give them something that meaningfully improves their productivity, that's worth a lot. The early chat products were somewhat useful. But the ROI really changed maybe a year ago, when the first really good coding models showed up.

Catherine: How do you know whether you are getting productivity wins from AI tools?

Patrick: We track a bunch of output metrics: pull requests, features shipped and lines of code. None of them is perfect on its own. I think of R&D as a big machine. You put resources in, you get features and code out, and you can measure how much more is coming out. In aggregate, we're close to doubling output with the same team. The teams that rebuilt their processes around AI are going a lot faster than that.

Catherine: When Databricks first rolled out AI coding tools, what did you get wrong?

Patrick: It's kind of funny because at the start, we had the opposite problem. Nobody wanted to try the new stuff. I was going around bugging people. So we did what everyone did, which was remove every barrier: the most expensive model, as many tokens as you want. I think that came from a good place. You're trying to get people over the hump.

Then people actually started using it, and we saw this exponential cost curve. These tools are all consumption-priced now, not per seat, so a single user can, in principle, spend an unbounded amount of money. They can run a little loop on the most expensive model and go to lunch. Maybe that loop is doing something really valuable, but maybe it’s just burning tokens. If your costs grow exponentially and your revenue doesn't, at some point, you have a problem. We got to the point where the costs were threatening to reverse the efficiency gains, which were the whole reason we did this.

That's when I got very involved personally. I compared notes with leaders at other technology companies who I knew were adopting AI at scale (Coinbase, Uber, Stripe, and others). Collectively, many of us were pursuing similar techniques. Today, at Databricks, our token spend per head is roughly flat now, even as total usage and value keep going up.

Catherine: Most companies' first instinct is a hard spend cap. You tried that. What happened?

Patrick: It's the obvious first move, and you do want the mechanism. But a hard stop is a bad experience. You cut someone off mid-task, and they lose their flow, maybe hours of work. And the people hitting the cap are often your best users. Cut them off, and some of them just go use a personal account, and now you can't see anything.

So we moved to friction that ramps up, and Unity Gateway handles all of it. First, a warning, then an approval, then we downshift you to a cheaper model so you can keep working. Actually cutting someone off is a last resort. We also send everyone a regular breakdown of their own spending with suggestions on where to save. That alone is worth about 10%. One company I know of puts the model and the cost right in every pull request. So it's basically public shaming if you use an expensive model for a small thing. I love it.

Catherine: You've written about four levers for bringing these costs down. Which one has had the biggest impact?

Patrick: Our favorite one is kind of boring: better, cheaper models keep coming out, and you move traffic to them. There are probably five models released every week between the proprietary and open source vendors. Not every one is a step forward on cost, but maybe one every week or two is. It's a rising tide. You get the same output for less money, and nobody has to change anything. No fancy routing, nothing.

To give you a sense of how fast this moves: one of the recent cheap models roughly matches what a frontier model could do about nine months ago, at around 1% of the cost per task. That's a 100x drop in under a year. That's still preliminary, but it's the direction.

The catch is you have to actually move. If a new model comes out and nobody in your company is using it, it's a tree falling in the woods. So we got good at evaluating new models fast and shifting workloads over when one is good enough. Because everything goes through Unity Gateway, we can make that switch in one place, and developers don't have to change anything. That's been the most impactful thing we've done, 50% or more on its own. Add routing, spend visibility, and cutting token overhead, and in some cases, our unit costs are down as much as 90%.

Catherine: Your team benchmarks coding agents against Databricks' own multi-million-line codebase. Why not just trust the public benchmarks?

Patrick: Public benchmarks don't tell you much about your own code. The tasks leak into training data, and they don't look like a big enterprise codebase. So we built our own from real pull requests in our repo, and we grade by actually running the tests. We don't use an LLM as the judge, because that tends to reward sounding right over being right.

Some of the results surprised people. An open source model, GLM 5.2, tied Opus 4.8 on quality at about a third less per task. One model that was 1.7x cheaper per token cost more per task, because it burned through more tokens. And the harness, the coding tool around the model, mattered about as much as the model. Same model, different harness, more than 2x difference in cost. Just tuning our harness and caching settings saved us close to 50%.

Catherine: The gap between the cheapest and most expensive models can be 100x. How should engineering leaders think about that range?

Patrick: Think of it like cars. There's the Lamborghini, the Honda, and the bicycle. You don't need the Lamborghini for every trip, and most coding work doesn't need the biggest model.

Astra was a good example. We rolled it out to every engineer, around 3,500 people, and as far as we know, we're the first company to share a rollout like that publicly. It was clearly better on the hard stuff, like system design. But spend went up about 60%, and it wasn't obviously helping on everyday tasks, which the existing models already handle fine. A lot of that was waste, people using Astra for things they should've used another model for. So we gave it its own budget in Unity Gateway. Use it for the hard problems.

Long term, I don't know which way this goes. Cheap models keep taking over more of the routine work, but people are also throwing harder and harder problems at AI. That's kind of the point. You want to be able to steer either way.

Catherine: You've argued that AI cost is an infrastructure problem, not a procurement problem. Why can't budgets and policy solve it?

Patrick: Budgets help, but a budget can't decide which model should handle a given request. That's routing. Renaming a component goes to a cheap model; a hard, open-ended problem goes to a capable one. Our Smart Router cuts average task cost by more than 30% at roughly the quality of the most expensive model. It's also allowing us to stop asking users to decide when to use the more expensive models… that just happens.

To do any of this you need a layer between your developers and the models. We built ours because we had to. All our coding tool traffic goes through one gateway, whether it's Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or Omnigent, our meta-harness. That's what let us actually see where the money was going. Then we realized every customer had the same problem, so we productized it as Unity Gateway. Thousands of customers use it now.

Catherine: Will routing end up as competitive as the models themselves?

Patrick: That's our view. As margins on the models get thinner, figuring out which model to use for what is a pretty interesting place to be. The routing models have to be tiny and fast. It's also just hard to do well. There are a lot of open research problems in the practical side of using these models, and I think there's real IP in getting it right.

Catherine: If you could give one piece of advice to a CTO staring at a growing AI bill, what would it be?

Patrick: Figure out where it's going. Most companies can't tell you what they're spending on AI by team or by model, let alone whether it's paying off. Put a gateway in front of your models so all the traffic goes through one place, and you can see it. Everything else gets easier after that. And don't slow down. The productivity gains are real. But this stuff compounds, and if you wait, the bill is going to be a lot bigger than you think.

Patrick's message to engineering leaders is that you don't have to choose between AI productivity and cost control. The companies getting this right keep broad access to the best models, test new models on their own code, move to cheaper ones as soon as they're good enough, and give developers visibility instead of walls. Underneath all of it is one control layer, a gateway, that makes AI spend something you can see and steer. At Databricks, that layer became Unity Gateway.

To learn more about how Databricks manages its own AI coding spend, read Patrick's blog "Managing AI Coding Costs at Scale," and try Databricks Unity Gateway.

entries.content:
AI Runtime enables developers to use NVIDIA frameworks, OSS models, and containers across clouds on Databricks without managing GPU infrastructure

by Tejas Sundaresan, Hanlin Tang, Julia Powell, Joel Caruso (NVIDIA) and Mayank Tahilramani (NVIDIA)

  • Databricks AI Runtime (AIR) is now Generally Available (GA), helping teams train and fine-tune models faster on serverless NVIDIA GPUs without the complexity of managing GPU infrastructure.
  • AIR supports NVIDIA NeMo and containers so teams can train and fine tune models on serverless NVIDIA GPUs alongside governed enterprise data.
  • Databricks uses NVIDIA Kumo open models to accelerate predictions from structured data and NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models to find relevant evidence from unstructured data, enabling agents to make informed decisions and take action within Databricks workflows.
  • Developers can leverage Genie Code, NVIDIA-specific Agent Skills and our joint Nemotron cookbooks to get started with model customization on AIR.

GPUs power today's most advanced AI workloads, from cutting-edge language models to multimodal AI systems and agents. Increasingly, enterprises are adapting open models to their own data and business needs. But securing GPU access is only part of the challenge. Teams also need to configure training jobs, govern data access, and manage GPU infrastructure, leaving less time to experiment with models and evaluate how well they meet business needs.

Databricks and NVIDIA provide a seamless path from enterprise data to customized AI models, from fine-tuning smaller models to large-scale distributed training. Through Unity Gateway, Databricks provides developers with governed access to frontier and open-source models. For teams that need to customize models, AI Runtime (AIR) brings NVIDIA’s AI software ecosystem and serverless GPUs to enterprise data. Teams can experiment, fine-tune, and evaluate models on AIR, then deploy them for real-time inference through Databricks Model Serving — all within the Databricks Platform, with less infrastructure and governance work to manage.

Today at GTC Berlin, Databricks and NVIDIA are expanding their collaboration to make it easier for enterprises to customize open models. Databricks AIR is now generally available: developers can use NVIDIA NeMo, NGC containers, and new Nemotron cookbooks to train and fine-tune open models on serverless NVIDIA GPUs. Together, these capabilities give teams more flexibility to adapt models to business-specific tasks and put them to work in applications and agents.

AI Runtime has unlocked model training and reinforcement learning on enterprise data that has traditionally been out of reach for machine learning engineers. With AI Runtime and NVIDIA's AI software ecosystem, teams can specialize open weight models such as Nemotron for their custom use cases and business context. With governed data access, ease-of-use for large scale training, and Genie Code for automated debugging, AI Runtime will accelerate the rise of customized models in enterprise.—Hanlin Tang, CTO for Neural Networks, Databricks
Agents are most valuable when grounded in how a business actually works — its data, workflows and expertise. NVIDIA and Databricks are bringing open models like Nemotron and Kumo directly to governed enterprise data, giving teams the models, tools and accelerated computing to build specialized agents that can reason over company knowledge, predict what comes next and take action.—Pat Lee, VP of Strategic Partnerships, NVIDIA

AIR provides serverless NVIDIA GPUs for training and fine-tuning, so developers can run their existing code and containers at scale without managing GPU infrastructure. With support for multi-node distributed training, teams can scale larger workloads across GPU nodes. NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand provides high-bandwidth, low-latency networking with remote direct memory access (RDMA), while NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) handles communication between GPUs. Databricks manages the underlying clusters and networking.

For example, an enterprise building a technical support agent could start with an NVIDIA Nemotron open model and fine-tune it on labeled support tickets using NVIDIA NeMo on AIR. The team could experiment with different training approaches and use MLflow to track results as they adapt the model to their specific support workflows.

Developers can prepare Lakehouse data and experiment in GPU-powered notebooks or through the AIR CLI, using high-performance data loading and standard environments that include PyTorch and CUDA. They can use distributed training frameworks or bring their own libraries and custom training loops.

When experiments are ready for repeatable execution, Lakeflow Jobs can orchestrate training alongside upstream data preparation and downstream evaluation, turning individual runs into repeatable workflows. Declarative Automation Bundles support CI/CD for deploying and updating those workflows.

MLflow tracks training experiments and GPU utilization, helping teams compare model results and compute performance. Unity Catalog governs access to training data, and native system tables provide visibility into CPU and GPU usage. Together, these integrations let teams use the data, governance, and operational tools they already rely on in Databricks.

Training and fine-tuning deep learning models takes more than GPU compute—teams also need flexibility in their frameworks, libraries, and environments. AIR now supports Docker and private registries, allowing developers to bring custom containerized environments to their GPU workloads.

Developers can use GPU-optimized containers from the NVIDIA NGC Catalog with the Databricks Artifact Registry to bring NVIDIA software into AIR. Environment caching helps these workloads start quickly, reducing setup overhead as teams iterate on training code and rerun experiments.

Developers can also install NVIDIA profiling tools to examine GPU execution and investigate performance bottlenecks. Alongside GPU utilization metrics tracked in MLflow, these tools help teams understand where training workloads spend time and identify opportunities to improve performance. Teams can tune their software and training code while AIR manages the underlying GPU infrastructure.

AIR supports customization beyond LLMs, including a validated fine-tuning workflow for NVIDIA Kumo Anomaly, an open research model for time-series anomaly detection, with MLflow tracking and Unity Catalog checkpoints. This supports NVIDIA’s Agent Knowledge Foundation vision of building an agent knowledge layer. Pairing Kumo-Anomaly with the Genie Ontology offers a path to context-aware agents that connect unusual patterns in time-series data with business meaning to help inform next steps.

With the release of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Super VL, Databricks customers can load, experiment with, adapt, and serve these models on Databricks from day one.

AIR supports model customization with NVIDIA NeMo and NeMo Automodel, enabling teams to use NVIDIA’s tools and frameworks on serverless NVIDIA GPUs. In the technical support agent example, this means developers could use these tools to fine-tune Nemotron on historical support tickets, helping the model better understand company-specific products, terminology, and troubleshooting workflows. Training stays connected to enterprise data and workflows in Databricks.

Genie Code can also help developers author and adapt the training script directly in a notebook. Developers can describe the changes they need, ask for help configuring a fine-tuning run, and work through errors as they arise. They can review and refine the suggested code before running it on serverless NVIDIA GPUs.

For fine-tuning, AIR combines optimized data loading, checkpointing, and training with integrated observability and debugging tools. Developers can track experiments and GPU metrics in MLflow and use Genie Code to:

  • Debug model code and investigate training errors.
  • Identify GPU performance bottlenecks, including memory issues and communication overhead.
  • Apply NVIDIA-specific guidance on CUDA, cuDNN, NCCL, and profiling tools.

After fine-tuning and evaluation, teams can deploy customized models to production through Databricks Model Serving. In our technical support example, the fine-tuned Nemotron model could power an agent that interprets incoming support requests and generates responses informed by the company's products and troubleshooting workflows. This completes the workflow from model customization on serverless NVIDIA GPUs to real-time inference.

To learn more, visit our web page, AIR documentation, and explore the Nemotron 3.5 SuperVL and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning cookbooks to get started with GPU training and fine-tuning on Databricks.

entries.summary: Today, we’re excited to announce the General Availability of AI Runtime (AIR), bringing...
entries.content:
Train foundation models faster on your enterprise data with fully managed GPU infrastructure

by Tejas Sundaresan, Jianwei Xie, Mike Del Balso, Hanlin Tang, Julia Powell and Cynthya Peranandam

  • AI Runtime is now generally available, bringing high-performance GPU infrastructure directly into Databricks.
  • Scale reliably and experiment faster with seconds-level launches, flexible environments, and integrated observability — without the overhead of managing GPU infrastructure.
  • Keep every training workload secure and governed with built-in Unity Catalog controls and workload isolation — in a new era of agent-led training.

Today, we’re excited to announce the General Availability of AI Runtime (AIR), bringing fully managed GPU infrastructure directly into Databricks so customers can train their most demanding models where their enterprise data already lives.

Too often, AI teams spend more time securing GPU capacity, managing failures, and waiting for experiments to launch than improving their models. Running GPU infrastructure separately from their Lakehouse adds governance gaps and puts sensitive training data at risk. As coding agents drive more training experiments, these bottlenecks and risks grow — making reliable, fast, and governed infrastructure essential.

AIR brings GPU infrastructure, developer tools, and data governance together so teams can train at scale, iterate faster, and secure every workload without managing a separate GPU stack. Hundreds of companies, including Tubi, Robinhood, PicPay, Merck, Flo Health, TinyFish, and FactSet, already use AIR to train and ship deep learning models to production, with use cases spanning healthcare, manufacturing, and consumer-facing agents. Our own Databricks AI Research team uses AIR to train the models behind KARL and AI Parse.

With AIR, customers can:

  • Train at scale with hassle-free GPU infrastructure: Serverless, on-demand access to advanced GPUs backed by reliable multinode training, optimized performance, and battle-tested by 100,000+ GPU-hour training runs.
  • Experiment faster with near-instant launch latency and easy debugging: Bring your own code, containers, and Ray workloads – and obtain seconds-level launch latency on RDMA-enabled GPUs. Environment caching and built-in debugging tools to save time on every training loop.
  • Secure and govern every GPU workload: AIR operates within the governance perimeter of Databricks and Unity Catalog, and is backed by years of investment in Serverless security. AIR helps ensure GPU workloads protect valuable training data, comply with access policies, and are tracked/auditable.

Managing GPU infrastructure requires significant operational overhead, from capacity planning and node maintenance to networking and monitoring.

With AIR, Databricks takes on the operational work of provisioning GPUs, maintaining healthy infrastructure, and optimizing the workload, so your team can focus on training:

  • Get the GPU capacity you need, on demand. Databricks handles GPU procurement, cluster configuration, and networking so your team can start training without building and operating a full GPU platform.
  • Scale with confidence on healthy infrastructure. Databricks runs dozens of checks for GPU and network health before and during training, so your workloads can scale to hundreds of GPUs reliably.
  • Efficient training by default: Built-in data loaders stream and cache training data to reduce time spent waiting on I/O. Use tools such as UCVolumeDataset to improve data throughput without building a custom loading pipeline.
Using Databricks AI Runtime, we moved our large-scale training from a single-node setup with 8 A100 GPUs to a multi-node setup with 16 H100 GPUs. This reduced training time from roughly seven days to 48 hours, a 3.5x speedup, making it much easier for our team to iterate on larger model experiments and train more efficiently.—Kostia Omelianchuk, Applied Research Scientist and Area Tech Lead, Superhuman

Use GPUs wherever you work

Access GPUs via CLI or interactively within Notebooks or IDEs. Your first workload just requires a single CLI command. With Databricks AIR Skills, migrating from a K8S or SLURM cluster just takes a single natural language prompt.

Working on TubiFM, we’ve collaborated closely with the Databricks team to refine the tooling for serverless GPU workloads. They’ve been very receptive to our feedback, and that collaboration has really paid off. Today, we’re very happy with the compute availability, ease of use, and how well everything fits into our existing Databricks environment.—Alexandre Salle, Principal ML Scientist, Tubi

Orchestrate GPU workloads with confidence with Lakeflow

AIR integrates natively with Lakeflow so you can keep GPU workloads in sync with upstream and downstream pipelines. Moving to production requires just a few extra lines of YAML, with built in priority/pre-emption that minimize idle GPU time and monitoring tools like Genie ZeroOps that lower operational toil.

Distributed training workloads are painful to set up and launch. AI teams waste time configuring training environments, waiting for GPU clusters to spin up, and debugging issues across the stack.

AIR helps you get from code to training in seconds. You can use pre-built environments or bring your own container, and benefit from highly optimized environment caching so you just need to build environments once. AIR is compatible with all major frameworks, including Ray, so you can bring code over with minimal configuration.  

Databricks AI Runtime lets us train where our data already lives, with the reliability, security, and performance we need for large-scale model training. We can spend less time managing GPU infrastructure and more time improving the models themselves.—Vladislav Nedosekin, Director of Engineering, Data & AI Platform, Flo Health

Launch your next experiment in seconds

When you iterate and develop a training script, every second of delay is felt repeatedly. And so, we’ve optimized every layer of the provisioning stack to make workloads, even large scale RDMA-enabled clusters with dozens of GPUs, spin up in seconds.

Debug distributed training in one place

We’ve built an entirely new observability experience in MLflow, the industry’s leading experiment tracking tool. With this new experience, debugging your logs, which stream seconds after submission, is as simple as adding 

–watch
 to your AIR command. For deeper investigation, you can use our new logs viewer, tailor-built for multinode training.
Databricks' AI Runtime greatly streamlined the process of training a custom Text To Formula (TTF) model. With no infrastructure setup or delays, it was easy to choose the right compute based on prompt size and output token generation. This allowed us to move quickly, maintain our Lakehouse workflows, and deliver a high-quality model with full governance, reducing time to setup, train and deploy our model from days to hours.—Nikhil Sunderraj, Principal Machine Learning Engineer, FactSet

Agentic debugging with built-in Genie Code

Genie Code is embedded into the entire user experience, and comes pre-packaged with agent skills to help you debug issues and optimize GPU training performance. These skills include insights that our research and performance teams discover, like how we reduced Qwen training time by 6x on AIR.

At Robinhood, AI Runtime helps our teams move from experimentation to training faster, without the infrastructure overhead. Fine-tuning is seamless, letting us train where our data lives while keeping governance and data controls built in. That means our engineers spend more time building better models and less time managing complex GPU setups.—Robert Macy III, Machine Learning Engineer, Robinhood
Databricks AI Runtime lets us scale distributed training on serverless GPUs across millions of records, right inside our existing data workflows. As more of the top 20 biopharma companies rely on our models to inform development decisions, that speed and simplicity lets our team keep improving the models instead of managing the infrastructure.—Eran Barash, VP of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, QuantHealth

Managing GPU infrastructure separately from enterprise data creates governance gaps, fragmented access controls, and unnecessary data copies. As agents run hundreds of training experiments in parallel, teams need to ensure sensitive data stays governed and workloads remain securely isolated, without relying on manual oversight. The OpenAI Huggingface incident underscores this risk. 

AIR extends your trusted data controls and governance to every GPU workload. Unity Catalog enforces consistent read/write permissions on all aspects of a GPU workload (data access, checkpoints, logs, etc.), so your GPU platform and data governance layer now speak the exact same language.

Isolate workloads and control network access

AIR is backed by years of investment in serverless security, isolation, and private networking. Unlike GPU isolation mechanisms that expose the host kernel, AIR has VM-level isolation, supports PrivateLink and serverless egress controls. Thus AIR offers much stronger protections for training workloads compared to conventional systems. 

Understand where your GPU budget goes

Track AIR usage and costs through Databricks billing system tables, alongside your other Databricks workloads. Use workload-level usage records to identify which training workloads consume your GPU budget and guide decisions about future runs. 

With Databricks AI Runtime and Serverless, we’ve been able to scale LLM training and inference more quickly, working with larger models, multiple H100 GPUs, and large volumes of data. The integration with our existing pipelines, together with Databricks’ orchestration and monitoring capabilities, has made the end-to-end workflow simpler and more efficient, reducing infrastructure complexity and development cycle time.—Vitor Rolim, Staff Machine Learning Engineer, PicPay
For us, training the model is only part of the problem. We need to know whether a change actually makes the agent better at completing real tasks, and then be able to get that improvement into production quickly. With AI Runtime, we can train on GPUs, evaluate with MLflow, and serve our web-native model without building a separate stack for every stage.—Zach Richardson, Head of AI, TinyFish

To help you get started, we’ve put together several template notebooks and starter guides:
