entries.title: Deploy RFD4-Proteina on Databricks
entries.summary: Bring RFD4-Proteina to your research data with AI-assisted development and serverless NVIDIA GPU compute....
entries.content:
Bring RFD4-Proteina, co-developed by the University of Washington Institute for Protein Design and NVIDIA, with research data, AI-assisted development and serverless GPU compute on Databricks.

by Srijit Chandrashekhar Nair, Mark Lee, Mayank Tahilramani (NVIDIA), Joel Caruso (NVIDIA) and Ian Kerman (NVIDIA)

  • Start with Genesis Workbench, the open, modular life sciences blueprint underpinning the RFD4-Proteina integration on Databricks.
  • Use Genie Code and domain-specific agent skills to develop and extend workflows,from preparing model inputs to analyzing generated candidates.
  • Execute GPU-intensive workloads with AI Runtime while connecting research data, experiment tracking, and governance on one platform.

Bring RFD4-Proteina to your research data with AI-assisted development and serverless NVIDIA GPU compute.

  • Get started with day-zero model support through Genesis Workbench, an open example blueprint for life sciences workflows.
  • Build and adapt pipelines with Genie Code, NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit skills, and coding-agent assistance.
  • Use Databricks’ generally available AI Runtime to execute supported GPU workloads alongside enterprise data, experiment tracking, and governance.

RFD4-Proteina, an NVIDIA BioNeMo open model co-developed with the University of Washington Institute for Protein Design, helps scientists turn ideas for useful proteins into designs they can test. NVIDIA and Databricks are bringing the model into Genesis Workbench on AI Runtime, giving developers a path to connect protein-design workflows with their research data.

Databricks AI Runtime (AIR) provides serverless NVIDIA GPU compute for supported workloads. The planned integration connects model execution with research data and repeatable workflows on Databricks, reducing the infrastructure overhead required to evaluate and adapt a new model.

Putting a model to work requires more than downloading weights. Developers need to prepare inputs, connect scientific tools, configure execution, and track results—all while protecting proprietary data. Databricks brings these steps into a shared environment, reducing the need to assemble and maintain a separate research stack.

"Drug discovery is a data problem before it's a compute problem. NVIDIA and the Institute for Protein Design are pushing the frontier of what's possible with models like RFD4-Proteina, and together, we're making sure life sciences teams can run those models on their own governed data, connected to their own experiments, without shipping sensitive IP outside their walls. You own the science. And the Databricks Platform makes sure it all runs in one secure, governed environment."—Mike Sanky, VP, Healthcare and Life Sciences, Databricks
"The hard part of protein design isn't generating candidates. It's choosing the few worth making in the lab. RFD4-Proteina designs a protein's sequence and its full atomic structure together, and it can be steered toward the properties a project needs, like stability or binding strength. Running it on Databricks, next to a team's own experimental data, helps scientists choose those candidates based on what their own experiments have already shown.—Anthony Costa, Director of Digital Biology, NVIDIA

RFD4-Proteina builds on the approach used in Proteina-Complexa, NVIDIA's generative model for designing protein binders that co-generates amino-acid sequences and all-atom structures in a single pass. RFD4-Proteina extends that joint generation approach with optional reward-guided search, letting researchers steer candidate design toward properties like thermostability or binding affinity. The planned integration expands on Genesis Workbench’s existing Proteina-Complexa workflows patterns,utilizing scoring models withreward functions specific to the problem at hand. Genesis Workbench has two built-in workflows using RFD4-Proteina for your reference: Antibody Design and Vaccine Design.

Pictured: Antibody Design in Genesis Workbench with NVIDIA RFD4-Proteina

Genesis Workbench offers an easy way to get started: its open, modular blueprint illustrates how to connect biological models with input preparation, candidate evaluation, and downstream analysis on Databricks. Developers can reuse individual components or adapt the implementation to their own scientific methods. 

Teams can store model weights in Unity Catalog volumes as governed MLflow models and reuse them across experiments. Teams can register fine-tuned models in Unity Catalog through MLflow, connecting model versions with configurations and artifacts. Access controls and network configuration should reflect where the model, scoring tools, and coding agents execute.

Using RFD4-Proteina through Genesis Workbench gives Databricks users the broader ability to connect research across disciplines: genomics analysis can inform a target, single-cell data can provide biological context, and protein-design or small-molecule workflows can support subsequent investigation. Genesis Workbench provides examples of these capabilities within a shared environment.

Databricks Genie Code helps developers build, debug, and adapt data and ML workflows using natural language. NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit skills add specialized instructions, scripts, and references for biological models and scientific tools, including structure prediction, protein design, molecular docking, and genomics analysis.

These skills can help a coding agent prepare inputs, invoke supported tools, inspect outputs, and assemble multi-step workflows. Developers can combine that guidance with their own data conventions, evaluation criteria, and experiment-tracking requirements.

Genesis Workbench also provides skills for Claude-based coding agents, offering another entry point: helping developers understand the blueprint, scaffold integrations for new models such as RFD4-Proteina, and tailor those integrations to a specific use case. This can accelerate the first implementation; dependency checks, testing, and scientific review remain part of the process.

A life science researcher could leverage prebuilt RFD4-Proteina workflows directly from Genesis Workbench or use Genie Code to create a Databricks Notebook for an ad-hoc experiment with a simple english prompt like:

“Design a nanobody (VHH) against PD-L1 using RFD4-Proteina framework conditioning: keep a real humanized framework (h-NbBCII10) fixed and design only the CDR loops onto the PD-1-blocking epitope. Run 8 iterations × 8 samples with ProteinMPNN on the CDRs and Boltz co-folding for binding; weight the reward toward binding (ipTM), fold confidence (pLDDT), developability (solubility, thermostability), and low anti-drug-antibody risk (MHC-II). Return the top designs with the reward trajectory and top-K complex PDBs."

Genie Code assists with implementation, while developers and researchers retain control by reviewing the code, selecting appropriate tools, and interpreting results.

AIR simplifies access to NVIDIA acceleration without requiring teams to provision and maintain separate GPU clusters. Developers can connect a notebook to Serverless GPU compute, select an NVIDIA H100 accelerator and a supported environment, and run their workload. The documented setup includes selecting the accelerator and base environment before applying the configuration.

This reduces the work of configuring GPU infrastructure and maintaining a base software environment,though teams still need to validate model-specific libraries and dependencies.

For supported biological foundation models, teams can also adapt BioNeMo Recipes to train or fine-tune on proprietary data using AIR’s serverless GPUs. BioNeMo Recipes provide reference implementations for accelerated training with familiar frameworks such as PyTorch and Hugging Face. 

Lakeflow orchestration, MLflow experiment tracking, and Unity Catalog governance connect execution to repeatable workflows and enterprise controls. Scientists can focus more on biology, while developers and platform teams spend less time managing infrastructure.

An example practical model lifecycle on Databricks can include:

  • Store model weights in a governed Unity Catalog volume for reuse.
  • Generate candidate molecules on AIR, or train and fine-tune where the model and recipe support it.
  • Track parameters, metrics, and artifacts with MLflow and register deployable models in Unity Catalog.
  • Deploy compatible models to GPU Model Serving endpoints, or orchestrate batch execution when that better fits the workload.
  • Connect outputs to research workflows through Genesis Workbench examples or your own pipelines.

For supported custom-model endpoints, scale-to-zero can reduce provisioned capacity during inactivity. Cold starts add latency, and GPU capacity is not guaranteed when an endpoint scales back up. Databricks recommends disabling scale-to-zero for workloads requiring consistent availability or response times.

Teams can choose the execution pattern that fits the research task, balancing runtime, cost, and availability requirements.

Across the workflow, teams can retain the configuration, model version, evaluation results, and artifacts needed to compare experiments. Computational evaluation supports candidate prioritization; laboratory validation remains essential.

Explore the Genesis Workbench repository and begin with one target, a defined design objective, and a small experiment. Use the example implementation and available agent skills to adapt the workflow, then execute and track it on AIR before expanding.

entries.title: MemCurrent: Designing Persistent Memory for Production Agents
entries.summary: AI tools have made it easy to vibe code agents. Building and maintaining an enterprise...
entries.content:
AI tools have made it easy to vibe code agents. Building and maintaining an enterprise agent in production, however, remains significantly more challenging. In particular, developers are often forced to make a trade-off between quality (getting good answers, especially on long-tail tasks) and efficiency (keeping cost and latency in check at scale). Oftentimes, techniques bring gains in one dimension at the cost of another.

Memory is a promising way to improve both at the same time. It can help agents carry useful context across tasks, such as user preferences, prior corrections, metric definitions, and successful workflows. In principle, this can improve accuracy, reduce repeated errors, and avoid unnecessary rediscovery. But more history is not necessarily better memory. Supplying every past interaction is costly and can introduce stale, conflicting, or irrelevant context. The central challenge is deciding what to retain, how to maintain it, and how to measure usefulness.

In this post, we introduce MemCurrent, a persistent memory architecture for production agents, which now powers the new Agent Bricks Memory and Genie. Agents read and write memory as they work, and an offline “dreaming” pipeline consolidates memory to keep it consistent and fresh. On our internal benchmark, built from realistic enterprise tasks, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate over having no memory, while using 31% fewer tokens and running 26% faster. The rest of this post covers how we designed and evaluated it, and what we learned along the way.

Figure 1. Pass rate vs. tokens per task on our Internal Memory Benchmark. MemCurrent is on the Pareto frontier, outperforming Mem0, PropMem, and OpenClaw memory on both dimensions.

There are three ways to wire memory into an agent. As a plugin (like our earlier work on MemAlign and Memory Scaling), memory is read and written automatically at fixed points in a session. As tools, the agent decides what and when to read and write. As an offline pipeline, memory is updated in the background on a schedule or trigger, and used in later sessions. Each comes with trade-offs:

Memory as a …

Triggered by

Time of computation

Pros

Cons

Plugin

Automatic

Online
  • Updates take effect immediately
  • Predictable behavior
  • Higher runtime cost and latency
  • Inflexible (e.g., wasting tokens even when memory isn't needed)

Tool

Agent

Online
  • Updates take effect immediately
  • Agent has flexibility
  • Higher runtime cost and latency
  • Quality constrained by agent capability
Pipeline Schedule or trigger Offline
  • Lower runtime cost and latency (async batched)
  • Updates arrive with a delay

Table 1. Three access patterns of memory: plugin, tool, or offline pipeline.

MemCurrent uses all three, each where it fits best.

Figure 2. Overview of MemCurrent.

MemCurrent has two types of memory: episodic memory, which stores raw session traces; and derived memory, which has the distilled learnings from these traces, stored as files in a structured knowledge base. An auto-generated 

memory.md
index sits at the top, describing the file structure and what each file contains.

Both episodic and derived memory live in a production-grade database that can scale to many users while delivering low-latency responses. Episodic memory is append-only, where a plugin logs each step as the session runs. Derived memory is a mutable table simulating a hierarchical file system, where writing happens in two ways. Agent tools (

add_memory, update_memory, delete_memory
) handle explicit requests like “Never write scripts in the /tmp dir”. An offline dreaming pipeline captures the rest, distilling implicit learnings from each new session into the relevant files. It also cleans up the whole store, splitting oversized files, merging duplicates, and resolving conflicts.

Reading works in layers. At session start, a plugin injects the memory index, so the agent knows what it knows before it begins. During the session, the agent has two tools that work across both memory types: 

search_memory
returns the top matches for a query (a step in a past trace, or a line in a memory file), and 
fetch_memory
returns the full entry by identifier (session ID or file path).

We start with three popular open-source benchmarks: LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and ConvoMem. All three test whether an agent can recall facts stated earlier in open-ended synthetic conversations.

In addition, we built an Internal Memory Benchmark from real Genie conversations, where users ask all kinds of questions about their data. As in Figure 3, we started from 12K+ sessions, mined 3K candidates containing memory-worthy signals, and drafted a follow-up question with scoring rubrics. The other sessions from the same user serve as fillers for the test case. An adversarial judge then checked each test case against 7 criteria, such as whether the knowledge is actually present, specific to the user, required to answer, natural, and verifiable. After a final manual review, the benchmark has a total of 114 test cases, with 29 users and 2,233 history sessions. 

Figure 3. How we built our Internal Memory Benchmark.

Here's an example:

Figure 4. An example test case from our Internal Memory Benchmark. In a past session, the user corrects the agent's choice of table and tells it to exclude background requests. Later, the agent faces a different but related question, and has to find that session among 100+ others and apply what it learned. The output is scored by an LLM judge based on a list of rubrics (some memory-dependent, some task-intrinsic).

Our benchmark differs from existing ones in three ways:

Enterprise domain. Existing benchmarks are open-ended chats about the lives of simulated personas. Ours is from real work in a data workspace, involving rich enterprise knowledge like table semantics, metric definitions, and workflows.

Memory feeds actions, not answers. Finding the right string in past conversations is not enough; agents must apply retrieved knowledge to complete multi-step tasks.

Diversity. Test cases span 5 memory types (profile, preferences, domain knowledge, projects, workflows) crossed with 11 scenarios (direct instruction, changing or outdated facts, multi-session aggregation, memory-independent questions, and more).

We compare MemCurrent with three open-source memory backends, Mem0, PropMem, OpenClaw memory, using the same underlying LLM. 

Open-Source Benchmarks. We pair each memory backend with a simple question-answering agent, built with two agent harnesses (LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK). We also run two baselines: a floor with no memory, and a ceiling with full context, where every past session goes into the agent's context. Across all three benchmarks, MemCurrent scores highest among all memory backends and stays on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. On average, MemCurrent (88.1%) performs on par with full context (87.8%) at ~12x fewer input tokens per question (8.4K vs 103K). On the two benchmarks with the longest histories, it even beats full context, where dumping everything into the prompt ends up confusing the agent.

Figure 5. Cost–accuracy1 trade-off of memory backends on (a) LoCoMo (19–32 sessions/sample), (b) LongMemEval (s split) (38–62 sessions/sample), and (c) ConvoMem (stratified subset of 500 samples, 100 sessions/sample). We use GPT 5.6 luna as the agent and memory model. All memory backends are run as a plugin, which automatically searches for related memories to the question and injects them into the agent context at session start.2 Accuracy is the mean over the LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK harnesses and 3 repeats. Cost is mean input tokens per question (log scale).

Internal Memory Benchmark. On our benchmark, the gap widens. Here, each memory backend runs inside our internal Genie, the same agent the benchmark sessions came from. The histories are too long to fit in context, so our ceiling is gold injection: injecting only the gold memories into the agent's context. Among all memory backends, MemCurrent has the highest pass rate (68.4%) and the lowest latency (252s) and token usage (418K), closing over 80% of the gap between no memory (22.3%) and gold injection (78.6%). Notably, while Mem0 was also on frontier on earlier benchmarks, it trails at 43.9% here with higher latency and cost. Compared to no memory, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate (22.3% → 68.4%) while making it 1.35x faster and 1.44x cheaper.

Figure 6. Pass rate, mean latency, and mean token usage per task on our Internal Memory Benchmark across 3 repeats. We use Claude Opus 4.6 as the agent model and GPT 5.6 sol as the memory model. All memory backends are provided as agent tools and a session-start plugin.

In addition to benchmark numbers, let's examine two examples of how MemCurrent helps in practice, from internal Genie sessions.

Example 1: Memory stops an occasional hallucination mistake. In Figure 7, a user asked the agent for the top 20 users of Product X over the past two months. The agent wrote a correct SQL query, but never read the actual execution results saved to a file. It still confidently produced a table with hallucinated content. Upon user feedback, the agent saved the lesson to memory. Next time, once the query ran, the agent read the results first and returned the right table. One memory correction kept a one-off slip from becoming a habit.

Figure 7. An anonymized example of how memory helps the agent avoid a repeated hallucination mistake.

Example 2: Memory saves computation on related tasks. In Figure 8, a user asked for “the top 5 SDP customers”. The agent had to figure everything out from scratch: what “SDP” stands for, which tables held usage data, and how to join and filter them. It took 11 tool calls, 8 subagents, and nearly six minutes. The agent saved these steps as a workflow file in memory, which it could reuse on related tasks. Later, the user asked a different question: how many SDP customers had more than 5K pipeline runs last month. Using the workflow, the agent answered with 2 tool calls and 1 subagent in 41 seconds. The question was new, but the path to the answer wasn't, and memory let the agent skip unnecessary exploration.

Figure 8. An anonymized example of how memory turns a 6 minute task into 41 seconds.

To understand what accounts for MemCurrent's superior performance, we ran ablations on our Internal Memory Benchmark for two design choices: memory types and extraction strategy.

Do we need both memory types? Episodic memory alone helps moderately: 35.8%, up from 22.3% with no memory. The raw history is useful, but the agent only searches it in about a third of test cases, though it passes 60% of those when it does. Derived memory avoids this issue, as the injected memory index at session start gives the agent information about what's available in memory and when to look, lifting pass rate to 66.1%. Adding episodic memory on top gives the best result, at 68.4%. The gain is small, but it suggests raw traces can recover details that distillation drops.

Figure 9. Pass rate by memory type.

What's a good memory extraction strategy? As shown in Figure 2, two channels extract derived memory: online tools and offline dreaming. When isolated, offline dreaming (63.5%) beats online tools (53.9%) by nearly 10 points. Their combination produces the highest pass rate at 66.1%. That supports a split of duties: dreaming handles background extraction and consolidation, while online tools make explicit requests take effect right away.

Figure 10. Pass rate by extraction strategy.

Memory is how an agent stops starting from zero. In this post, we introduced MemCurrent, a memory architecture for production agents that combines episodic memory and derived memory, with three access patterns: plugins to log and load context automatically, tools the agent calls on demand, and an offline dreaming pipeline that consolidates memory in the background.

Across all benchmarks we ran, MemCurrent improves quality and efficiency at the same time, the trade-off we set out to break. On open-source benchmarks, it matches full context performance at about 12x fewer input tokens. On our Internal Memory Benchmark, built from real data work, it triples the agent's pass rate over no memory while also making it faster and cheaper.

The ablations point to where the value comes from. Derived memory does most of the work, and episodic memory adds a smaller boost by recovering details that distillation drops. Combining online tools with offline dreaming makes the best extraction strategy: explicit requests take effect immediately, while dreaming distills implicit learnings and consolidates the store in the background.

Beyond the numbers, memory provides a knowledge base that isn't tied to a single agent or LLM. It can move with users to new agents or LLMs, and could seed knowledge shared across their organization, a direction we are exploring next.

We're bringing these findings to drive improvements across Databricks products:

For agent developers. Agent Bricks is Databricks' developer platform for building custom agents. MemCurrent is built into Agent Bricks' Memory offering, powered by Lakebase. The offering includes:

  • Session store for episodic memory
  • Memory store for derived memory
  • An automatic dreaming pipeline
  • Tracing and evaluation of agent quality, including the impact of memory
  • A CLI which helps you quickly get started with an end-to-end sample agent with all of the above in <10 minutes

Get started building your custom agent today.

For Databricks Genie users. Genie is an interface where Databricks users can converse with their data in natural language. MemCurrent is already in action behind the scenes, helping to improve answer quality while reducing response latency and cost.

Get started with Genie.

Authors: Veronica Lyu, Wenhao Zhan, Sam Havens, Ziyi Yang, Jenny Sun, Qinxin Wang, Nihit Desai, Sirui Sun, Ankit Mathur, Jane Zhang, Yi Liu, Jialu Liu, Michael Bendersky, Matei Zaharia, Xing Chen

We thank Jonathan Li, Rishabh Singh, Andy Zhang, Kenneth Choi, Will Tipton, Cassie Cao, Siddharth Murching, Sue Ann Hong, Pranav Sukumar, Neo Ni, Shanshan Zheng, Chung Wu, and our internal user study participants for their feedback and support throughout this project.

1 The latency is similar (4-7s/question) across all memory backends, as most questions are answerable within a single hop.

2 We find plugin-based memory sufficient for the existing benchmarks. Results from adding tools are strictly dominated and thus omitted.

entries.title: Introducing Agent Memory on Databricks
entries.summary: Today we're introducing agent memory on Agent Bricks, Databricks' agent developer...
entries.content:
by Sirui Sun and Nihit Desai

Today we're introducing agent memory on Agent Bricks, Databricks' agent developer platform. Agent memory improves agent quality while decreasing costs and latency by storing critical facts, preferences, and workflows that an agent should remember. It's available in Beta today, runs on Lakebase for high reliability and low latency, and is built on Databricks' latest memory research.

Without memory, agents risk rediscovering key facts, forgetting user preferences, and repeat mistakes it was already corrected on. In response, many developers are rolling their own memory solutions, but run into numerous design questions - for example, where should memories be stored? How should memories get synthesized? And once generated, how should they be retrieved?

To address this, Databricks Agent Memory is built on the MemCurrent architecture, pioneered by Databricks Research. MemCurrent combines three access patterns: plugins to log and load context automatically, tools the agent calls on demand, and an offline dreaming pipeline that consolidates memory in the background. All of this is served with extremely low latency using Lakebase. In our internal benchmarks, implementing this memory architecture tripled agent pass rate on real enterprise tasks while using 31% fewer tokens. 

Agent Memory joins the rest of Agent Bricks, including agent hosting, Databricks Sandbox, Unity Gateway, pre-built MCP servers, and tracing and evaluation, providing developers all the infrastructure capabilities needed to build production agents.

Two problems show up as soon as an agent moves from a demo to daily use.

  • Costs climb with every rediscovery. A stateless agent re-derives what it figured out yesterday: which table holds usage data, what an internal acronym means, which join actually works. In one real session from our research, an agent took 11 tool calls, 8 subagents, and nearly six minutes to answer a question about one product's top customers. The next day, it would have done all of that again.
  • Agents never get personal. A user states a preference, corrects a mistake, or explains how their team defines a metric, and the agent forgets it when the session ends. Either the user repeats themselves, or the agent repeats the mistake.

Agent developers, and the platform teams that run their agents, have two common workarounds. Each one trades one problem for another:

  • Replaying the full history into context works until histories get long. On open-source memory benchmarks, full context used about 12x more input tokens per question than a well-designed memory at the same accuracy, and on the longest histories it scored worse, because irrelevant turns confused the agent.
  • Building memory yourself on object storage or a vector database means owning extraction, deduplication, retrieval, and access control. Memories go stale, contradictory facts pile up, and no one can tell which memory caused a bad answer.

What teams need is memory that makes agents cheaper and more personal at the same time, without standing up another system to get it.

Figure 1. Agent Memory on Agent Bricks. The agent appends each turn to managed sessions, recalls and saves memories directly, and a memory pipeline distills sessions into long-term memory in the background.

Agent Memory has three parts:

  • Managed sessions record each conversation as an ordered history of messages, tool calls, and results, in your framework's native format.
  • Managed memory keeps what's worth remembering: profile, preferences, domain knowledge, and workflows. At the start of a session, the agent loads an index of what is known in memory. During the session, it finds details with hybrid keyword and semantic search.
  • Memory pipelines distill sessions into memory in the background, on demand or on a regular basis in the background. They extract durable facts and preferences, remove duplicates, and replace facts that newer conversations contradict.

Everything runs on Lakebase, Databricks' serverless Postgres, provisioned in your workspace and operated by Databricks. This ensures that storing and retrieving memories is lightning fast, and that your stores can scale along with your agent traffic.

Agent Memory is a production implementation of MemCurrent, the memory system described in MemCurrent: Designing Memory for Enterprise Agents. Our researchers’ central finding is that memory works best in two layers: a raw record of what happened, and a distilled record of what's worth remembering, kept current by a background process rather than written ad hoc by the agent mid-task.

Built that way, memory improved quality and efficiency at the same time. Agents passed about three times as many tasks as agents without memory, finished faster, and used fewer tokens. The same infrastructure already powers memory in Genie, Databricks' natural-language experience for business users.

Figure 2. Agents with and without memory on Databricks' internal memory benchmark of enterprise data tasks. Source: MemCurrent research.

  • Lower cost per task. Agents skip work they've already done. In the example above, once the workflow was saved to memory, the agent answered a related follow-up question in 2 tool calls and 41 seconds, down from 11 tool calls and nearly six minutes.
  • Personalization that persists. Preferences, corrections, and team-specific definitions carry across sessions, scoped to each user, so people stop repeating themselves.
  • Mistakes that stay fixed. Agents remember their mistakes, and can avoid making the same mistake twice - saving valuable time and tokens.
  • Memory you own and control. Sessions and memories live in your Lakebase project, independent of any single agent framework. Developers can read, export, and delete the entries an agent keeps about each user, and give a memory pipeline instructions that steer what it retains, such as "keep durable customer preferences; ignore one-off debugging notes."
  • One platform for the whole loop. The same agent uses models through Unity Gateway, deploys with the Agent Bricks CLI, and is traced and evaluated with Agent Bricks' tracing, with memory included.

None of this requires new infrastructure on your side. The Agent Bricks CLI can help you deploy an agent with memory and sessions in minutes.

From then on, your agent's next conversation with each user starts with what it learned from the previous ones. For more info, see the quickstart to create a new agent with memory, or our tutorial for adding memory to an existing agent.

Agent Memory is one part of Agent Bricks, Databricks' agent developer platform for building, running, and improving custom agents at scale, with any model, framework, or harness. Explore Agent Bricks to see the rest of the platform.

  • Build a stateful agent in under 10 minutes with the Agent Bricks CLI documentation.
  • Add memory and sessions to an existing agent with the agent memory and sessions documentation.
  • Read the research behind it in MemCurrent: Designing Memory for Enterprise Agents.

entries.title: How Hamlet uses Databricks Lakebase Postgres to test changes against production data
entries.summary: Hamlet, an AI-powered platform that makes local government decision-making accessible...
entries.content:
A conversation with Hamlet CEO Sunil Rajaraman and engineers Erich Douglass and Jeff Hui

by Sara Steffen

  • Hamlet gives every pull request its own Lakebase Postgres branch of production data, so engineers test changes against the data that caused a bug without touching production.
  • AI coding agents run the pipelines and check their work on each branch before a person approves the merge.
  • Hamlet is exploring Lakebase Search for vector and text search in Postgres, branching for object storage and a home for longer agentic jobs.

Hamlet, an AI-powered platform that makes local government decision-making accessible and searchable, uses Databricks Lakebase Postgres to give every pull request its own branch of production data. Engineers and AI coding agents test changes against real data without touching production, and a person still approves every merge.

I spoke with CEO Sunil Rajaraman, Lead Developer Erich Douglass and Senior AI Engineer Jeff Hui about how they work.

Hamlet is an AI-powered technology platform that makes local government decision-making accessible and searchable. By indexing and transcribing thousands of city council, planning commission, and zoning board meetings across the U.S., Hamlet allows real estate developers, journalists, researchers, and citizens to instantly search meeting transcripts, track local policy developments, and set up real-time alerts for specific topics, addresses, or businesses.

Sara Steffen: Hamlet indexes meetings from more than 7,200 governing bodies across every state. What does that data landscape look like, and why is it so hard to make sense of?

Sunil Rajaraman: There are 19,000 city governments, 3,000 county governments and roughly 80,000 special districts in the United States. Pick any two of their websites and they won’t look alike. That’s the original sin of local government. A handful of CMS providers decided every site should be different, and the result is an internet of government that’s completely balkanized. Hamlet pulls all of it together and standardizes it.

Sara: Hamlet describes itself as a civic intelligence platform. How is that different from a transcription tool, and why does the distinction matter?

Sunil: A lot of govtech companies are an arbitrage of municipal data. They write brittle scrapers for 1998-era websites and put a modern coat of paint on top. Scraping and storing the data doesn’t add much on its own. You have to tell a story, and it has to be based on fact. That means knowing who’s speaking and how they feel about an issue. If you’re a developer, you want to know whether a council member will approve your housing project, why or why not, and what history the city has that might make it hesitate.

Look at permitting. A lot of venture money has gone into permitting data, and permitting timelines have still gotten worse over the past decade. Many companies have built monuments to the symptoms. We want to get to the underlying problem, which is understanding people. The question we’re trying to answer is how cities fundamentally work.

Sara Steffen: What makes local government data so difficult to work with?

Sunil Rajaraman: Pick any two of their websites and they won’t look alike. Hamlet pulls it all together and standardizes it.

Erich Douglass: You can’t just integrate with one provider. Seven or eight of them cover about 75% of the market. After that it’s a massive long tail of custom setups. Sometimes a clerk uploads a PDF of the agenda. Sometimes they scan a paper copy and upload that. You get some really weird artifacts.

Sara: What do customers need from that data?

Sunil: Our customers are private companies like real estate developers, data center developers and retailers. Nearly all of them are trying to get a project approved faster or find a new opportunity. Without Hamlet, someone sits through hours of meetings, waits for their project to come up and watches the officials’ body language. We identify who spoke, take you to the timestamp and show you the receipts.

Erich: They also want precedent. Has a project like theirs been approved or rejected before? Why? What changes did the council ask for? If we can show what’s really going on, that’s a lot of value.

Sara: How do you help customers trust the insights they find?

Jeff Hui: We use it in almost every part of the process. Early on, Hamlet did this work by hand, and that doesn’t scale to thousands of places. For a lot of these governments, the video is the primary source of truth. Getting it into a structured form we can use is the most important part. The average meeting runs about three and a half hours. Nobody wants to watch all of it. AI points people to the parts worth their time, and the video is always there to back it up. We can show exactly what was said, which a lot of AI systems struggle to do.

Sara: How do you identify speakers accurately across thousands of meetings?

Jeff: Context makes the biggest difference. For speaker identification, we know which council or committee is meeting and who was on it at the time. That helps with names, which are hard to get right even for a person listening to a recording. You can’t hand a model a video and hope for the best. You have to collect everything around it that helps it make the right call. It’s a forever challenge.

Sara: How do you check the AI’s interpretation of what officials say?

Sunil: Accurate transcription comes first. For sentiment, we use multiple AI models to confirm a comment is about a given topic, say data centers. Then they look at the surrounding context to decide whether it’s for or against.

You also have to define what pro and anti mean before you ask. Take policing. What does being for it mean? We put a lot of care into those questions. Several models now review every sentiment figure before we publish it, and we require high confidence.

Lakebase is the managed Postgres database Hamlet uses to give each pull request its own branch of production data. Engineers can test changes against the data that caused a bug without touching production, while AI coding agents run the pipelines and check their work before a person approves the merge. The team says its previous test-data setup could take several hours per engineer each week.

Sara: Why did you choose Lakebase, and what changed for your team?

Erich: We had a pretty standard setup on AWS RDS, with one production instance and one staging instance. A lot of our work is tuning data pipelines against very specific data. For every pull request, we’d spend 15 to 30 minutes getting staging into the right state before we could run validations. We’re a small team, and velocity matters to us more than almost anything.

Data branching was the feature that sold us. Every pull request now gets its own branch of production data, connected to its preview environment. When the preview deploys, it’s ready. We can test against production data and even write to it without touching production.

Autoscaling helps too. On RDS, a bigger instance meant a migration that could take a couple of hours. Now we move a slider and get twice as big an instance.

Jeff: The 15 to 30 minutes was the best case, when you happened to copy exactly the right data. Each engineer could spend several hours a week keeping test data current, including cloning pieces of production locally to chase down issues. Now when we hit a bug, we have the exact data that caused it, and we can check the fix against that same data.

Sara: How does Lakebase change the way your AI coding agents work?

Jeff: Branches make our workflow a much better fit for AI coding agents. Each pull request is isolated from production. We give an agent like Claude or Codex access to its branch and let it run its own checks. It runs the data pipelines to completion and looks at whether the change does what it should. Every pull request gets that first pass from an agent. By the time a person looks at it, we’re already fairly confident it works. A human still approves the merge. More and more of the rest is automated, and Lakebase is a big part of what makes that possible.

Sara: What are you exploring next with Lakebase?

Erich: Right now most of our data lives in a relational database, and search runs on a separate vector database. The two drift out of sync. Testing search becomes the old staging problem again. I’ve been trying out Lakebase Search which combines vector and text search in Postgres, and having it all in one place has been great.

Sara: Beyond search, what would you like to simplify next?

Erich: Branching has worked so well that we’d love the same thing for the large files we keep in object storage. Every developer has test buckets next to one shared production bucket, and managing state across them is hard.

Jeff: We’re also looking at where to run longer agentic jobs. Part of our ingestion uses AI to drive a web browser and find the right content on government sites. Some runs take a few minutes. Others take 30 or 40, and our current AWS Lambda setup has a 15-minute limit.

Hamlet’s work starts with the original meeting recording, so customers can trace an AI insight back to what an official said. Lakebase supports the engineering workflow behind that experience: branches of production data let developers and coding agents test changes without touching production, while people still approve the final merge. For a small team working across thousands of governing bodies, that means less time preparing test data and more time improving the product.

How can you create and automatically delete a Lakebase branch for every pull request?

Add two steps to your continuous integration (CI) pipeline: create a branch from production when a pull request (PR) opens and delete it when the PR merges or closes. You can script both steps with the Databricks CLI and run them from a tool such as GitHub Actions. Set an expiration, a time-to-live (TTL), when you create the branch so it deletes itself even if the cleanup step never runs. See the branch-based development workflow tutorial for a full example.

How does database branching work in Postgres?

A Lakebase branch is an independent Postgres environment that starts with the schema and data of its parent and shares storage with it through copy-on-write. Only changes made on the branch are written separately, so creating a branch does not depend on database size. Standard Postgres creates a new database by copying an existing one, which duplicates the data. Lakebase database branches avoid that copy, and changes in a child branch never affect its parent.

How do you roll out database branching to a development team?

Start with one branch per pull request, the pattern Hamlet uses, then extend branching to the rest of your workflow. Each pattern replaces a shared staging database with isolated environments.

  • One branch per pull request: CI creates the branch when the PR opens and deletes it when the PR closes.
  • One branch per developer: each engineer gets an isolated environment with production-like data, and you can reset it from its parent to pull in the latest schema and data.
  • One branch per test run: each CI run starts from a fresh, isolated database with no leftover state.

How much does a Lakebase branch cost?

Cost depends on compute and storage. Each branch has its own compute, which scales to zero when idle, so you pay only for active compute hours. For storage, an expiring branch is billed only for the data that changes on it, while a permanent branch with no expiration is billed for its full data size. Keep an expiration on short-lived branches. See branch expiration for the options.

Can AI coding agents test on a Lakebase branch without touching production?

Yes. Each branch is isolated from production, so an agent can apply migrations, run tests and retire the branch when it finishes. A person still approves the merge, and schema changes move to the parent branch through migrations in code rather than by merging the branch.
